final.title: Exit plans get expensive when the workflow stays in your head
final.body:
If you are an owner-operator, the cost of an exit plan is often not the plan itself. It is the scattered work sitting behind it.

When repeated customer questions, lead follow-up, and invoice or data work live in your head, they also live in your calendar. That leaves less room for the boring but necessary exit work: documenting the process, training someone else, or preparing a clean handover. The 8–10 hours-a-week scenario is only a persona example, not a market statistic, but it shows the pressure clearly.

The practical decision is simple: pick one recurring workflow and ask whether it is repeatable enough to handle in a bounded way. A good test is whether the task has the same inputs, the same checks, and the same expected output most of the time. If it does, that is the first place to look.

Bareni’s normal sequence is a free 30-minute diagnostic, then a one-page pilot proposal, then a paid MVP in days. Those timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. The point is not to automate everything. It is to remove one repetitive task so the owner keeps final approval, and can spend more time on exit preparation instead of cleanup.

That is usually where the real cost shows up: not in the exit plan, but in the work you still have to finish before it makes sense.

final.title: Exit plans get expensive when the workflow stays in your head
final.body:
If you own a small business, the cost of an exit plan is not just legal fees or broker time. It is the work you still have to do before the business can be handed over cleanly.

That is why I would start with one bounded workflow decision: pick the single recurring task that eats the most time and repeats in a predictable way. In the persona scenario, that could be customer questions, lead follow-up, or invoice/data work. The point is not to automate everything. It is to find the one routine that is still living in your head.

If that workflow is not documented, it will sit in the way of process notes, training, and a clean handover. That is true whether you are thinking about succession, a sale, or simply reducing how much of the business depends on you.

A practical next step is simple: this week, write down the one task you would least want to explain from scratch to someone else. Then check whether it has a clear trigger, a clear output, and a clear human approval point. If it does, it may be a good candidate for a bounded automation discussion. If it does not, it probably needs cleanup first. Boring, but useful.

State one concrete, bounded workflow decision and one practical next step. For example, frame the decision as whether to map a single recurring workflow before planning the exit, then ask the owner to identify that workflow and note what happens if they leave it unbuilt.
